grammarTopics.title: Perfect Continuous Tenses
grammarTopics.explanation:
### What they have in common
All perfect continuous tenses use **been + verb-ing** and look back from a reference point (now, a past moment or a future moment) to stress the **duration** of an activity or the **activity itself** rather than its result.

| Tense | Reference point | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| present perfect continuous | now | *I've been studying for three hours.* |
| past perfect continuous | a moment in the past | *I'd been studying for three hours when you called.* |
| future perfect continuous | a moment in the future | *By six, I'll have been studying for three hours.* |

### Simple or continuous?
Use the **simple** perfect for results, numbers and completed actions (*I've written three emails*), and for stative verbs (*I've known her for years*). Use the **continuous** for ongoing or recently finished activities, especially with *for, since, how long, all day, lately*.

> **Catatan:** Pola *sudah ... selama/sejak* dalam bahasa Indonesia biasanya diterjemahkan dengan perfect continuous jika aktivitasnya masih berlangsung. Jangan pakai present continuous (*I am waiting since...* ✗).

positive: She has been working here since March.
They had been waiting for an hour when the doors finally opened.
By June, I'll have been teaching for ten years.
negative: I haven't been sleeping well lately.
He hadn't been feeling well, so he stayed at home.
interrogative: How long have you been learning English?
Had they been arguing before you arrived?

grammarTopics.comparison: Present perfect simple = result or number (I've painted two rooms). Present perfect continuous = activity or duration (I've been painting all day). Stative verbs (know, own, believe) normally take only the simple form.

mistakes.wrong: I am waiting here since 10 a.m.
mistakes.right: I have been waiting here since 10 a.m.
mistakes.why: An activity that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect (continuous).

mistakes.wrong: We have been knowing each other since school.
mistakes.right: We have known each other since school.
mistakes.why: Know is a stative verb and is not used in continuous forms.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the present perfect continuous form of the verb in brackets.
exercises.text: My hands are covered in flour because I ___ (bake) all morning.
answers: have been baking
exercises.explanation: The flour is the present result of an activity that lasted all morning → **have been baking**.

exercises.context: By the time the rescue team found them, the climbers ___ in the snow for two days.
exercises.explanation: Duration up to a moment in the past (*by the time the rescue team found them*) → **had been waiting**.
*Four emails* is a number of completed items, so we need the simple form: **has written**.

exercises.prompt: Combine the information in one sentence.
exercises.sentence: Tomi started playing the guitar when he was eight. He is eighteen now, and he still plays.
exercises.cue: Use the present perfect continuous. Begin with: Tomi ...
answers: Tomi has been playing the guitar for ten years.
Tomi has been playing the guitar since he was eight.
Tomi's been playing the guitar for ten years.
Tomi's been playing the guitar since he was eight.
exercises.explanation: Started in the past + still continuing → **has been playing ... for ten years / since he was eight**.

grammarTopics.title: Future Continuous and Future Perfect
grammarTopics.explanation:
### Three advanced future forms
| Form | Use | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| future continuous (**will be + -ing**) | an action in progress at a future time; polite questions about plans | *This time tomorrow, I'll be flying to Jayapura.* |
| future perfect (**will have + past participle**) | an action completed before a future time | *By 2030, the city will have built a new metro line.* |
| future perfect continuous (**will have been + -ing**) | duration up to a future time | *In May, I'll have been living here for ten years.* |

### Time expressions
*this time tomorrow/next week, at 8 p.m. tomorrow, by + time, by the time + present simple, in + period*.

### Related expressions
*be about to* (very soon), *be due to* (scheduled), *be likely to* (probable), *be bound to* (certain).

> **Catatan:** Setelah *by the time / when / before*, gunakan **present simple**, bukan *will*: *By the time you arrive, I'll have finished.* Kata *by* di sini berarti *paling lambat*.

positive: At nine tomorrow, we'll be sitting our final exam.
By the end of the month, they will have moved into their new flat.
negative: Don't worry, I won't be using the car tonight.
The workers won't have finished the road by Friday.
interrogative: Will you be passing the post office on your way home?
Will you have finished the report by Monday?

grammarTopics.comparison: Future continuous = in progress at a future moment (At 10, I'll be writing). Future perfect = finished before a future moment (By 10, I'll have written it).

mistakes.wrong: By the time we will arrive, the show will have started.
mistakes.right: By the time we arrive, the show will have started.
mistakes.why: Use the present simple after by the time.

mistakes.wrong: This time next week I will lie on a beach.
mistakes.right: This time next week I will be lying on a beach.
mistakes.why: An action in progress at a future time needs the future continuous.

exercises.text: Please don't phone me between two and four tomorrow afternoon. I ___ an exam.
exercises.explanation: An action in progress during a future period → **will be taking**.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the future perfect form of the verb in brackets.
exercises.text: By the end of this year, Ana ___ (save) enough money for a new laptop.
answers: will have saved
exercises.explanation: Completed before a future time (*by the end of this year*) → **will have saved**.

exercises.context: In June, my parents ___ in this house for exactly twenty years.
exercises.explanation: Duration (*for twenty years*) up to a future point (*in June*) → **will have been living**.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the correct order to make a question.
exercises.explanation: Question form of the future perfect: **Will + subject + have + past participle**.

grammarTopics.title: Third and Mixed Conditionals
grammarTopics.explanation:
### Imagining a different past
| Conditional | If-clause | Result | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| third | had + past participle | would/could/might have + past participle | *If we had left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.* |
| mixed (past → present) | had + past participle | would + infinitive | *If I had taken the job, I would live in Singapore now.* |
| mixed (present → past) | past simple | would have + past participle | *If I were braver, I would have spoken up.* |

### Conditions without if
*unless* (= if not), *provided/providing (that), as long as* (= only if), *supposing* (= imagine), *otherwise* (= if not, referring back). Formal inversion: *Had I known, I would have helped.*

> **Catatan:** Jangan pernah memakai *would have* di klausa if: *If I would have known* ✗ → *If I had known* ✓. Perhatikan kata keterangan waktu (*now, yesterday*) untuk memilih jenis conditional.

formulas.label: Third conditional
formulas.pattern: If + had + past participle, would/could/might have + past participle

formulas.label: Mixed: past → present
formulas.pattern: If + had + past participle, would + infinitive (now)

formulas.label: Mixed: present → past
formulas.pattern: If + past simple, would have + past participle

positive: If she had studied law, she would have become a judge.
If I hadn't missed the bus, I would be at the meeting now.
negative: We wouldn't have got lost if we had taken a map.
interrogative: What would you have done if the bank had refused your loan?
Would you be happier now if you had stayed in your hometown?

grammarTopics.comparison: Second conditional = unreal present (If I had time, I'd help). Third = unreal past (If I'd had time, I'd have helped). Mixed conditionals combine the two time frames.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would have come.
mistakes.right: If I had known, I would have come.
mistakes.why: The if-clause uses the past perfect, never would have.

mistakes.wrong: Unless you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.
mistakes.right: Unless you hurry, you'll miss the train.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the correct form. Use the words in brackets.
exercises.text: If the taxi ___ (not / arrive) on time, we would have missed our flight.
answers: hadn't arrived
had not arrived
exercises.explanation: Third conditional if-clause: **hadn't + past participle**.

exercises.context: I never learned to drive, so I couldn't take my friend to the airport yesterday.
exercises.text: If I ___ how to drive, I ___ you to the airport yesterday.
exercises.explanation: A general present situation (not knowing how to drive) → **knew**; a past result (*yesterday*) → **would have driven**.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using as long as.
exercises.sentence: You can use my car, but only if you return it by six.
exercises.cue: Begin with: You can use my car ...
answers: You can use my car as long as you return it by six.
You can use my car so long as you return it by six.
exercises.explanation: *Only if* = **as long as** + present simple.
An imaginary situation after *supposing* uses the past simple (like the second conditional): **Supposing you lost your passport...**

grammarTopics.title: Advanced Passive and Causative
grammarTopics.explanation:
### The passive in all forms
The passive is **be + past participle**; only *be* changes: *is done, is being done, was done, has been done, had been done, will be done, must be done, needs to be done, being done*.

### Causative
**have/get + object + past participle** = someone else does it for you (*I had my car serviced*), or something bad happens to you (*She had her bag stolen*). **get + person + to-infinitive** = persuade someone.

### Passive reporting structures
- *It is said/believed/thought that + clause*
- *Subject + is said/believed + to + verb* (same time) / *to have + past participle* (earlier)

> **Catatan:** Awalan *di-* dalam bahasa Indonesia = *be + V3*. *Sedang di-* = *is being + V3*; *sudah di-* = *has been + V3*; *konon/diyakini* = *is said/believed to*.

formulas.label: Passive
formulas.pattern: Subject + be (any form) + past participle (+ by agent)

formulas.label: Reporting passive
formulas.pattern: Subject + is said/believed + to + verb / to have + past participle

positive: The bridge is being repaired at the moment.
We had our roof replaced last year.
The castle is believed to have been built in the 12th century.
negative: The results haven't been published yet.
This medicine shouldn't be taken with alcohol.
interrogative: Has the parcel been delivered yet?
Where do you get your hair cut?

grammarTopics.comparison: I repaired the bike (I did it). I had the bike repaired (a mechanic did it). I got my dad to repair the bike (I persuaded him).

mistakes.wrong: The accident was happened at night.
mistakes.why: Happen is intransitive and cannot be passive.

mistakes.wrong: I cut my hair at the salon yesterday.
mistakes.right: I had my hair cut at the salon yesterday.
mistakes.why: Use the causative when a professional does it for you.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the passive form of the verb in brackets.
exercises.text: The new hospital ___ (open) by the mayor next week.
answers: will be opened
is going to be opened
is being opened
exercises.explanation: A future action with the focus on the hospital → **will be opened** (future passive).

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the sentence so that it means the same.
exercises.sentence: People think that the fire was started deliberately.
answers: The fire is thought to have been started deliberately.
exercises.explanation: Earlier action + passive meaning → **to have been + past participle**: *The fire is thought to have been started deliberately.*

exercises.context: We don't clean the windows ourselves. We ___ them cleaned every three months.
exercises.explanation: Causative: **have + object + past participle** → *We have them cleaned.*
Modal passive: **must be + past participle** → *must be filled in*.

grammarTopics.title: Reporting Verbs and Reported Commands
grammarTopics.explanation:
### Patterns after reporting verbs
| Pattern | Verbs |
| --- | --- |
| + to-infinitive | agree, offer, promise, refuse, threaten, claim |
| + object + to-infinitive | advise, warn, remind, persuade, encourage, invite, tell, ask, order, urge |
| + -ing | admit, deny, suggest, recommend |
| + preposition + -ing | apologise for, insist on, object to |
| + object + preposition + -ing | accuse of, blame for, congratulate on, thank for |
| + that-clause | explain (to sb), complain, point out, announce, admit, deny, agree |

### Without backshift
Keep the original tense when the reporting verb is present (*She says she's busy*), when the information is still true, or for general facts.

> **Catatan:** Kesalahan paling umum: *suggest someone to do* ✗ → *suggest doing / suggest that someone (should) do* ✓, dan *explain me* ✗ → *explain to me* ✓.

positive: The landlord agreed to lower the rent.
She accused him of lying.
He pointed out that the contract wasn't signed.
negative: She warned us not to swim there.
interrogative: Did they ask you to wait outside?

grammarTopics.comparison: Tell + person (He told me to wait). Say (+ to person) (He said to me that...). Ask + person + to (requests). Ask + if/whether (questions).

mistakes.wrong: She suggested me to take a taxi.
mistakes.why: Suggest is not followed by object + to-infinitive.

mistakes.right: He told me not to worry.
mistakes.why: Reported negative commands use not to + verb.

exercises.prompt: Choose the verb that fits the pattern.
exercises.text: The shop assistant ___ checking the stockroom for my size.
exercises.explanation: **suggest + -ing** is correct. *Offer* and *promise* are followed by a to-infinitive (*offered to check*).

exercises.sentence: "Don't forget to bring your passport," my mother said to me.
answers: My mother reminded me to bring my passport.
My mother reminded me to take my passport.
exercises.explanation: **remind + object + to-infinitive**. *Don't forget to...* becomes *reminded me to...*

exercises.prompt: Complete the text with words from the bank.
exercises.text: The director congratulated us ___ winning the contract and thanked the team ___ working so hard. Then he warned us ___ to relax too much.
answers: on
for
not
exercises.explanation: **congratulate on**, **thank for**, **warn + object + not to**.

exercises.prompt: Yesterday my teacher said, "The library closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays." It is still true. Which report is correct?
options: My teacher said that the library closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays.
My teacher said that the library had closed at 8 p.m. on weekdays.
My teacher told that the library closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays.
My teacher said me that the library closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays.
exercises.explanation: The information is still true, so the present tense is fine. *Told* needs an object, and *said me* is wrong.

grammarTopics.title: Advanced Relative Clauses
grammarTopics.explanation:
### Types
| Type | Example |
| --- | --- |
| non-defining (commas, no *that*) | *My aunt, who lives in Bali, is a painter.* |
| with prepositions (formal) | *the town in which I grew up* |
| with prepositions (informal) | *the town I grew up in* |
| reduced: active → -ing | *the woman standing by the door* |
| reduced: passive → past participle | *a temple built in the 9th century* |
| the first/last/only + to-infinitive | *the first person to arrive* |
| comment clause | *He was late, which annoyed everyone.* |
| quantifier + of whom/which | *three sisters, all of whom are doctors* |

> **Catatan:** Setelah koma, jangan pakai *that*. Setelah preposisi, gunakan *whom* (orang) atau *which* (benda). *Most of whom* = sebagian besar dari mereka (orang).

positive: Mr. Tan, whose paintings hang in the gallery, is ninety.
The man sitting in the corner is a famous poet.
She has two brothers, both of whom are engineers.
negative: The museum, which wasn't open on Mondays, now opens every day.
interrogative: Is this the book you were telling me about?
Who was the first person to climb the mountain?

grammarTopics.comparison: Defining clauses identify (My sister who lives in Bali = one of several sisters). Non-defining clauses add information (My sister, who lives in Bali, = my only sister).

mistakes.wrong: The festival, that takes place in August, is famous.
mistakes.right: The festival, which takes place in August, is famous.
mistakes.why: That cannot be used in non-defining clauses.

mistakes.wrong: I have many friends, most of them live abroad.
mistakes.right: I have many friends, most of whom live abroad.
mistakes.why: Use most of whom after a comma to make one correct sentence.

exercises.text: Our new manager, ___ I met for the first time yesterday, seems very friendly.
exercises.explanation: A person, object of *met*, in a non-defining clause → **whom** (or *who* in informal style).

exercises.sentence: Ali has two sisters. Both of them are doctors.
exercises.cue: Begin with: Ali has two sisters, both ...
answers: Ali has two sisters, both of whom are doctors.
exercises.explanation: People → **both of whom**.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reduced relative clause with the correct form of the verb in brackets.
exercises.text: The documents ___ (send) to you last week contained an error.
answers: sent
exercises.explanation: Passive meaning (*which were sent*) → past participle **sent**.

segments: He failed his driving test again,
exercises.explanation: To comment on a whole clause, use **, which** (not *what*).

grammarTopics.title: Modal Perfects: Speculation and Criticism
grammarTopics.explanation:
### modal + have + past participle
| Modal perfect | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| must have | almost certain it happened | *She must have left already.* |
| can't/couldn't have | almost certain it didn't happen | *He can't have seen us.* |
| might/may/could have | perhaps it happened | *They might have got lost.* |
| should have | good idea, but it didn't happen | *You should have called.* |
| shouldn't have | bad idea, but it happened | *I shouldn't have said that.* |
| could have | possible, but it didn't happen | *You could have been hurt!* |
| needn't have | happened, but wasn't necessary | *You needn't have bought flowers.* |

*Didn't need to + infinitive* = it wasn't necessary (usually it didn't happen).

> **Catatan:** Kebalikan *must have* adalah **can't have**, bukan *mustn't have*. Dalam percakapan, *have* diucapkan lemah: *must've, should've* — tetapi jangan menulis *must of*.

positive: The streets are wet; it must have rained.
You should have told me earlier.
negative: She can't have forgotten; I reminded her twice.
We needn't have hurried; the train was late.
interrogative: Could he have taken the wrong bus?
Should I have called the police?

grammarTopics.comparison: must have = deduction (He must have taken the wrong road). should have = criticism (He should have taken the other road).

mistakes.wrong: She mustn't have heard the news.
mistakes.right: She can't have heard the news.
mistakes.why: For negative deductions, use can't have.

mistakes.wrong: I should have went to bed earlier.
mistakes.right: I should have gone to bed earlier.
mistakes.why: Use the past participle after have.

exercises.text: Rani ___ my message. Her phone was switched off all day.
exercises.explanation: The phone was off, so it's (almost) impossible → **can't have received**.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence using the words in brackets.
exercises.text: We took a taxi, but the station was only five minutes away. We ___ (needn't / take) a taxi.
answers: needn't have taken
need not have taken
exercises.explanation: The action happened but was unnecessary → **needn't have taken**.

exercises.sentence: It was a mistake not to back up the files.
answers: We should have backed up the files.
We should have backed the files up.
exercises.explanation: Regret about something that didn't happen → **should have + past participle**.

exercises.prompt: "He might have taken the wrong train." How sure is the speaker?
options: It was necessary for him to take it.
exercises.explanation: **Might have** expresses a possibility, not certainty.

grammarTopics.title: Linking Words: Contrast, Purpose, Result and Addition
grammarTopics.explanation:
### Choosing the right linker
| Function | + clause | + noun / -ing | between sentences |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| contrast | although, even though, whereas, while | despite, in spite of | However, Nevertheless, On the other hand |
| purpose | so that (+ can/could/will/would) | to / in order to / so as to + verb | — |
| result | so ... that, such ... that | as a result of | Therefore, As a result, Consequently |
| addition | — | in addition to, besides | Furthermore, Moreover, In addition |

### Punctuation
*However, therefore, moreover* start a new sentence (or follow a semicolon) and are followed by a comma.

> **Catatan:** Jangan gabungkan *although* dengan *but*. *Despite* tidak pernah diikuti *of* atau klausa lengkap. *In addition to* diikuti **-ing**.

formulas.label: Contrast
formulas.pattern: Although + clause, clause / Despite + noun/-ing, clause

formulas.label: Purpose
formulas.pattern: clause + so that + subject + could/would / in order to + verb

formulas.label: Result
formulas.pattern: so + adjective + that / such + (a) + adjective + noun + that

positive: Despite the rain, the match went ahead.
She saved money so that she could travel.
It was such a long film that I fell asleep.
negative: We left early so as not to miss the train.
interrogative: Why did you go even though you were ill?

grammarTopics.comparison: Although + clause (Although it rained...). Despite + noun/-ing (Despite the rain / Despite feeling ill...). However + new sentence (It rained. However, ...).

mistakes.wrong: Although it was late, but we kept working.
mistakes.right: Although it was late, we kept working.
mistakes.why: Don't use although and but together.

mistakes.wrong: Despite of the cost, they bought it.
mistakes.right: Despite the cost, they bought it.
mistakes.why: Despite is never followed by of.

exercises.text: ___ the fact that he had no experience, he got the job.
exercises.explanation: **Despite the fact that + clause**. *Although* would not be followed by *the fact that* here.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using so as not to.
exercises.sentence: He drove slowly because he didn't want to have an accident.
answers: He drove slowly so as not to have an accident.
exercises.explanation: Negative purpose → **so as not to + verb**.

exercises.text: The traffic was ___ heavy that we missed the start of the film.
answers: so
exercises.explanation: **so + adjective + that** shows result.
Don't use *but* after an *even though* clause: **Even though the evidence was weak, the jury found him guilty.**

grammarTopics.title: Wishes, Preferences and It's Time
grammarTopics.explanation:
### Unreal past forms with present meaning
| Structure | Use | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| wish / if only + past simple | unreal present | *I wish I had more time.* |
| wish / if only + past perfect | past regret | *I wish I hadn't said that.* |
| wish + would | annoying habit / desired change | *I wish he would stop shouting.* |
| would rather + bare infinitive | own preference | *I'd rather stay in.* |
| would rather + subject + past simple | preference about others | *I'd rather you didn't smoke.* |
| it's (high/about) time + subject + past simple | it should happen now | *It's high time we left.* |

> **Catatan:** Bentuk lampau di sini tidak berarti masa lalu; itu menunjukkan sesuatu yang **tidak nyata** atau **belum terjadi**. Jangan pakai *I wish I would* atau *wish ... would have*.

formulas.label: Past regret
formulas.pattern: Subject + wish / If only + subject + had + past participle

formulas.label: Complaint
formulas.pattern: Subject + wish + other subject + would (not) + verb

formulas.label: Preference
formulas.pattern: Subject + would rather + subject + past simple

positive: I wish I had listened to your advice.
It's time we went home.
I'd rather you came tomorrow.
negative: I wish you wouldn't interrupt me.
I'd rather not talk about it.
interrogative: Do you ever wish you had studied abroad?
Would you rather eat in or go out?

grammarTopics.comparison: I wish I knew (present) vs I wish I had known (past). I wish you would listen (habit/change) vs I wish you were here (state).

mistakes.wrong: I wish I would have a bigger flat.
mistakes.right: I wish I had a bigger flat.
mistakes.why: Don't use I wish I would; use the past simple for a present state.
Use the past simple after it's time + subject.

exercises.text: I wish I ___ the bus this morning. I was late for my interview.
exercises.explanation: A past regret (*this morning*) → **wish + past perfect**: *hadn't missed*.

exercises.prompt: Complete using the words in brackets.
exercises.text: I'd rather ___ (not / talk) about it right now, if you don't mind.
answers: not talk
exercises.explanation: Negative of *would rather* + bare infinitive → **would rather not talk**.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using high time.
exercises.sentence: You should start revising now. You've left it very late.
exercises.cue: Begin with: It's high time you ...
answers: It's high time you started revising.
It is high time you started revising.
It's high time you started revising now.
It's high time you began revising.
exercises.explanation: **It's high time + subject + past simple**: *It's high time you started revising.*

options: I wish you would stop tapping your pen.
I wish I would stop tapping my pen.
I wish you stop tapping your pen.
I wish you would to stop tapping your pen.
exercises.explanation: Complaint about someone else's habit → **wish + you + would + bare infinitive**.

reading.title: Rooftop Farms Take Root in Port Selatan
reading.body:
PORT SELATAN — Above the noise of one of the busiest shopping streets in Port Selatan, rows of tomatoes, chillies and spinach are growing where air-conditioning units once stood. The rooftop of the old Merdeka Department Store, which closed in 2019, has been turned into the city's largest urban farm, and it is expected to produce around four tonnes of vegetables this year.

The project was set up by a group of young engineers who had been looking for ways to reduce the distance food travels before it reaches people's plates. “Most of the vegetables sold in our markets have been transported for hundreds of kilometres,” said co-founder Dita Prameswari, 29. “We wanted to show that a city can feed itself, at least partly.”

The farm uses a hydroponic system, in which plants grow in water rich in nutrients instead of soil. According to the team, this method uses up to 70 per cent less water than traditional farming, although this figure has not been independently confirmed. Rainwater is collected from the roof, and solar panels power the pumps.

Not everyone is convinced. Some local farmers have complained that the project receives support from the city council while they struggle with rising costs. “It's a nice idea, but rooftops will never replace real farms,” said Bambang Wirawan, who grows rice outside the city. Building experts have also warned that many older roofs are not strong enough to carry the weight of water and equipment, and that inspections should be carried out before similar farms are built.

Despite these concerns, the council has announced that it will offer grants to building owners who want to install green roofs. Officials believe that by 2030, more than fifty rooftops in the city will have been converted. The farm's vegetables are currently sold to nearby restaurants, and a weekly market for residents is due to open next month.

For Dita, the project is about more than food. “When people see vegetables growing in the middle of the city, they start thinking differently about where their food comes from. That's the real change we want.”

glossary.meaning: hidroponik (menanam tanpa tanah, dengan air bernutrisi)
dikonfirmasi oleh pihak lain yang netral

questions.prompt: What is the article mainly about?
options: A rooftop farm in a city centre and people's reactions to it
The closure of a department store in 2019
A conflict between rice farmers and engineers
How to build a hydroponic system at home
questions.explanation: The article describes the rooftop farm, how it works, criticism of it and the council's plans (main idea). Gagasan utama mencakup seluruh teks, bukan satu detail.

questions.prompt: Where does the farm get the energy for its pumps?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: *solar panels power the pumps*.

reading.title: Why We Regret What We Didn't Do
reading.body:
Regret is one of the most common negative emotions that people report, yet psychologists have only relatively recently begun to study it systematically. A key distinction in the research is between regrets of action (things we did and wish we hadn't done) and regrets of inaction (things we didn't do and wish we had).

Earlier studies suggested that, in the short term, people tend to feel worse about their actions. If you make a rude comment at a meeting, for example, you are likely to regret it intensely that evening. Over longer periods, however, the pattern appears to reverse: when people look back on their lives, they mention missed opportunities far more often than mistakes. Typical examples include not studying harder, not travelling, or not spending enough time with family.

A study carried out at Northfield University asked 600 adults aged 30 to 80 to list their biggest regrets. Around two-thirds of the regrets described were regrets of inaction. The researchers proposed two explanations. First, people usually take steps to repair the consequences of their actions, by apologising, for instance, whereas inaction leaves nothing to repair. Second, when we imagine what would have happened if we had acted, the imagined outcome is often unrealistically positive, which makes the regret stronger.

It should be noted that the study relied on people's memories, which are known to be unreliable, and that all the participants came from one country. Cultural factors may influence what people regret; in societies that place great value on family duty, for example, regrets about relationships might be more common than regrets about career choices.

Nevertheless, the findings have practical implications. Some psychologists argue that regret, although painful, can be useful if it motivates people to change their behaviour. The authors of the Northfield study concluded that people who are unsure whether to take an opportunity might benefit from asking themselves a simple question: “Which choice am I more likely to regret in ten years' time?”

reading.title: The Four-Day Week: Fad or Future?
reading.body:
Imagine finishing work on Thursday afternoon and not returning until Monday, without any cut in pay. For a growing number of employees, this is no longer a fantasy. Over the past few years, companies in several countries have been experimenting with a four-day working week, and many say they have no intention of going back.

Supporters argue that a shorter week makes staff happier and healthier. Because employees have more time to rest, they are less likely to suffer from burnout and they take fewer days off sick. What is more, some firms claim that productivity has actually risen, since people waste less time in unnecessary meetings when they know their time is limited. A software company in Eastport, which introduced the scheme two years ago, reports that it has received three times as many job applications since the change.

On the other hand, critics point out that the model does not suit every industry. Hospitals, schools and shops cannot simply close for an extra day, so they would need to hire more staff in order to cover the missing hours, which would increase costs. Others worry that squeezing five days of work into four could lead to longer, more stressful days, especially for employees who were already struggling with heavy workloads. There are also concerns that customers might be frustrated if they cannot contact a business on Fridays.

Many of the success stories so far come from office-based companies whose work can be measured by results rather than by hours. It is therefore too early to say whether the idea could work across the whole economy. Some experts suggest a more flexible approach: rather than a fixed four-day week for everyone, employers could let staff choose how to organise their hours, provided that targets are met.

Whatever happens, the debate has forced many organisations to ask an important question: are long hours really the same as hard work?

reading.title: The Missing Manuscript
reading.body:
When Professor Hana Kirana arrived at the Old Harbour Library on Monday morning, she knew immediately that something was wrong. The glass case in the reading room, which had held the library's most valuable object, a 300-year-old manuscript of local poems, was empty.

There was no sign of a break-in. The doors had been locked all weekend, the alarm had not gone off, and the glass had not been broken. Someone must have opened the case with a key, Hana thought. But only three people had keys: Hana herself, the head librarian, Mr. Darmawan, and the cleaner, Bu Sari.

Mr. Darmawan was horrified when he heard the news. “It can't have been Bu Sari,” he said. “She's worked here for twenty years. And I was at my daughter's wedding in Bandung all weekend. Two hundred guests saw me there.”

Hana went to look at the case again. On the floor next to it, she noticed something small: a drop of blue wax. The library used blue wax to seal important letters, but the wax was kept in Mr. Darmawan's office, and his office had been locked too.

Then she remembered something. On Friday afternoon, a visiting researcher had asked to see the manuscript. Mr. Darmawan had opened the case for him and had then left the room for a few minutes to answer the phone. Hana checked the visitors' book. The researcher had signed his name as “Dr. A. Wirya”, but the address he had written did not exist.

“He might have made a copy of the key while you were out of the room,” Hana told Mr. Darmawan. “Wax is the easiest way to do it. You press the key into soft wax, and you have a perfect mould.”

Mr. Darmawan went pale. “I left my keys on the table,” he admitted. “I should never have left him alone.”

Three weeks later, the police tracked down “Dr. Wirya” in another city. The manuscript was found in his flat, undamaged. Hana insisted on putting it back in the case herself, and this time she had the lock changed.

listening.title: Second Careers: From Banking to Baking

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Welcome back to Second Careers. My guest today is Rudi Santoso, who spent twelve years working in a bank before opening a bakery in Malang. Rudi, what made you change?

script.speaker: Rudi
script.text: Honestly, I'd been feeling bored for years, but I was too afraid to leave. Then the bank was reorganised, and my department was closed. If that hadn't happened, I'd probably still be sitting behind a desk today.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: So, in a way, losing your job was a turning point.

script.speaker: Rudi
script.text: Exactly. At the time it felt like a disaster, but in hindsight it was the best thing that could have happened. I took a six-month baking course, and I'd been baking bread at weekends since I was a teenager, so I wasn't starting from zero.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Do you have any regrets?

script.speaker: Rudi
script.text: Just one, really. I wish I'd made the move earlier. I spent so many years waiting for the perfect moment, and of course it never comes. I also should have learned more about accounting before I started. The first year was hard because I'd underestimated the costs.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: What advice would you give listeners who are thinking about a career change?

script.speaker: Rudi
script.text: Try it out before you jump. Do a short course, help out at a friend's business, test the idea. And talk to your family. I couldn't have done it without my wife's support.

speaking.title: My City in 2050
speaking.prompt: A local radio station has asked listeners to predict what their city will be like in 2050. Make at least four predictions about transport, housing, work and technology, and show how certain you are about each one.
speaking.sampleAnswer: I think by 2050 my city will have built a proper metro system, so traffic jams will probably be much less common. Most people will be working from home at least part of the week, which is likely to change the city centre: many offices may well become flats. Housing is bound to be more expensive because more people will have moved here from the countryside. However, I doubt that we'll have flying taxis. They're too noisy and dangerous.

speaking.title: A Turning Point

speaking.sampleAnswer: A real turning point for me was failing my first university entrance exam. At the time, I was devastated. But because I failed, I spent a year working in a hotel, and that's where I discovered that I loved hospitality. If I hadn't failed the exam, I would never have taken that job, and I wouldn't be studying hotel management now. In hindsight, failing was the best thing that could have happened to me.

speaking.title: Complaining at a Hotel Reception

speaking.title: Debate: Should Under-16s Use Social Media?

speaking.sampleAnswer: On the one hand, social media helps teenagers stay in touch with friends and find information about their interests. What is more, many young people learn useful digital skills online. On the other hand, there is growing concern that it can affect sleep and self-esteem, and young users may not be aware of the risks of sharing personal information. Although a total ban would be difficult to enforce, I think on balance there should be stricter age checks, so that younger children are better protected.

speaking.title: Job Interview: Strengths and Experience

In my current job, I'm responsible for organising weekly events for hotel guests, and I've dealt with everything from booking musicians to handling complaints. I'm good at working under pressure, and I'm very familiar with planning software. Last year I came up with a new system for managing bookings, which cut our costs by around fifteen per cent. speaking.title: Pronunciation: Weak Forms in Modal Perfects
speaking.prompt: Read these sentences aloud, using the weak form of have /əv/: "You should've told me." "She must've forgotten." "They might've got lost." "We could've won." "He can't've seen us." Then make three sentences of your own about a recent mistake.
speaking.sampleAnswer: You should've told me. She must've forgotten. They might've got lost. We could've won. He can't've seen us. My own sentences: I should've checked the train times. I must've left my umbrella at the café. My friend might've been waiting for ages.
tips: In natural speech, have in modal perfects sounds like /əv/, not /hæv/.

writing.title: For-and-Against Essay: Working from Home
writing.instructions: "Working from home is better for employees than working in an office." Write a balanced essay discussing both sides of this statement and give your own opinion in the conclusion. Use four paragraphs and a range of linkers for contrast, addition, purpose and result.
writing.modelAnswer:
Since the start of the decade, millions of people have been working from home at least part of the week. Many believe this is a positive change, while others feel that the traditional office still has important advantages.

On the one hand, working from home saves time and money. Employees no longer need to commute, so they can spend more time with their families or on exercise. Furthermore, many people find that they can concentrate better at home, as there are fewer interruptions than in a busy open-plan office. As a result, some companies report higher productivity.

On the other hand, working from home can be lonely. Although video calls are useful, they cannot fully replace face-to-face contact with colleagues. What is more, it can be difficult to switch off when your home is also your workplace, which may lead to longer working hours and even burnout. Young employees, in particular, may miss opportunities to learn from more experienced colleagues.

In conclusion, working from home offers clear benefits in terms of flexibility and time. Nevertheless, it does not suit everyone. On balance, I believe a mixed system is best, in which employees spend two or three days in the office so that they can stay connected while still enjoying the advantages of remote work.

writing.title: Opinion Paragraphs: Should Museums Be Free?
writing.instructions: Write your opinion on the question: "Should national museums be free for everyone?" Give at least two reasons with examples, mention one opposing argument and explain why you disagree with it. Include at least two relative clauses and one passive structure.
writing.modelAnswer:
In my opinion, national museums should be free for everyone. Museums protect our cultural heritage, which belongs to all citizens, not only to those who can afford a ticket. When entry is free, families on low incomes, many of whom would otherwise never visit, can learn about their history and traditions.

Secondly, free museums are good for education. Schools can organise visits without asking parents to pay, and young people who are interested in art or history can return as often as they like.

It is sometimes argued that museums need ticket money in order to survive. However, I believe that this problem could be solved in other ways. Museums could be funded by the government, and visitors could be asked to make voluntary donations. Shops and cafés inside museums also earn money.

In short, our heritage should be enjoyed by everyone, not just by those who can pay for it.

writing.title: Summary: The Four-Day Week

One company also reports that it attracts more job applicants. However, critics argue that the model is unsuitable for industries such as healthcare, education and retail, where extra staff would be needed. They also fear that longer working days could increase stress. The writer concludes that it is too early to judge and mentions a more flexible alternative based on meeting targets.

vocabulary.definition: an agreement in which both sides accept less than they wanted; to make such an agreement

vocabulary.definition: to make someone believe that something is true

vocabulary.definition: to discuss something formally in order to reach an agreement

vocabulary.definition: a plan or suggestion, often a formal one

vocabulary.definition: the traditions, buildings and culture of a society that come from the past

examples.en: Batik is an important part of our cultural heritage.
examples.id: Batik adalah bagian penting dari warisan budaya kita.

vocabulary.definition: to keep something in its original state or in good condition

examples.en: The old town has been beautifully preserved.
examples.id: Kota tua itu dilestarikan dengan indah.

vocabulary.definition: something that a person or event leaves behind for the future

vocabulary.definition: famous and admired for a special skill or quality

vocabulary.definition: an object made by people, especially one of historical interest

examples.en: The museum displays artefacts from the 10th century.
examples.id: Museum itu memamerkan artefak dari abad ke-10.

vocabulary.definition: belonging to a place originally rather than coming from somewhere else

examples.en: The region has more than twenty indigenous languages.
examples.id: Wilayah itu memiliki lebih dari dua puluh bahasa asli.

vocabulary.definition: a piece of information that helps to solve a problem or mystery

examples.en: The footprint was the only clue the police had.
examples.id: Jejak kaki itu adalah satu-satunya petunjuk yang dimiliki polisi.

vocabulary.definition: a reason for doing something, especially a crime

examples.en: Nobody could understand his motive for the attack.
examples.id: Tidak ada yang bisa memahami motifnya melakukan serangan itu.

vocabulary.definition: proof that someone was somewhere else when a crime happened

examples.id: Alibinya dikonfirmasi oleh tiga orang saksi.

vocabulary.definition: to reach a conclusion by thinking about the facts you have

examples.en: From the evidence, the detective deduced that the thief had a key.
examples.id: Dari bukti itu, detektif menyimpulkan bahwa pencuri memiliki kunci.

vocabulary.definition: to disappear suddenly and completely

examples.en: The ship vanished without a trace.
examples.id: Kapal itu lenyap tanpa jejak.

vocabulary.definition: the state of being extremely poor

examples.en: Education is one of the best ways to reduce poverty.
examples.id: Pendidikan adalah salah satu cara terbaik untuk mengurangi kemiskinan.

vocabulary.definition: an unfair situation in which some people have more money, rights or chances than others

examples.en: The report highlights growing inequality between rich and poor regions.
examples.id: Laporan itu menyoroti ketimpangan yang makin besar antara wilayah kaya dan miskin.

vocabulary.definition: treating a person or group unfairly because of their race, gender, age, etc.

examples.en: The law protects workers from discrimination.
examples.id: Undang-undang itu melindungi pekerja dari diskriminasi.

vocabulary.definition: causing a lot of disagreement or strong feelings

examples.en: The new tax is highly controversial.
examples.id: Pajak baru itu sangat kontroversial.

vocabulary.definition: to make a determined effort to deal with a difficult problem

examples.en: The government must tackle unemployment among young people.
examples.id: Pemerintah harus mengatasi pengangguran di kalangan anak muda.

vocabulary.definition: help (often money) given by the state to people who need it; general health and happiness

examples.en: Animal welfare is a growing concern for consumers.
examples.id: Kesejahteraan hewan menjadi perhatian yang makin besar bagi konsumen.

vocabulary.definition: involving a lot of sitting and not much physical activity

examples.en: A sedentary lifestyle can lead to health problems.
examples.id: Gaya hidup yang kurang bergerak dapat menyebabkan masalah kesehatan.

vocabulary.definition: the quality of not doing or having too much of something

examples.en: Coffee is fine in moderation.
examples.id: Kopi tidak masalah asalkan tidak berlebihan.

vocabulary.definition: money that is paid back to you, for example when you return a product

examples.en: I returned the faulty kettle and asked for a refund.
examples.id: Saya mengembalikan ketel yang rusak dan meminta pengembalian uang.

vocabulary.definition: not working correctly or not made correctly

examples.en: The fire was caused by faulty wiring.
examples.id: Kebakaran itu disebabkan oleh kabel yang rusak.

vocabulary.definition: money paid to someone because they have suffered loss, injury or a problem

examples.en: Passengers received compensation for the delayed flight.
examples.id: Penumpang menerima kompensasi atas penerbangan yang tertunda.

vocabulary.definition: a person who starts their own business

examples.en: The young entrepreneur set up her first company at 22.
examples.id: Wirausahawan muda itu mendirikan perusahaan pertamanya pada usia 22 tahun.

vocabulary.definition: to find new people to work for a company; a new member of staff

examples.en: We're recruiting three new sales staff.
examples.id: Kami sedang merekrut tiga staf penjualan baru.

vocabulary.definition: the money a company or government receives

examples.en: The company's revenue rose by ten per cent last year.
examples.id: Pendapatan perusahaan naik sepuluh persen tahun lalu.

vocabulary.definition: to introduce a new product or start an activity; the event of doing this

examples.en: The app will be launched in September.
examples.id: Aplikasi itu akan diluncurkan pada bulan September.

vocabulary.definition: a move to a more important job in the same organisation; advertising activity

examples.en: She got a promotion after only a year.
examples.id: Dia mendapat kenaikan jabatan setelah hanya setahun.

vocabulary.definition: large or important enough to have an effect or be noticed

examples.en: There has been a significant increase in online sales.
examples.id: Ada peningkatan signifikan dalam penjualan daring.

vocabulary.definition: to judge how good, useful or successful something is

examples.en: We need to evaluate the results before we decide.
examples.id: Kita perlu mengevaluasi hasilnya sebelum memutuskan.

vocabulary.definition: an idea that is suggested as an explanation but has not yet been proved

examples.en: The results supported the researchers' hypothesis.
examples.id: Hasil penelitian mendukung hipotesis para peneliti.

examQuestions.context: I'm exhausted. I ___ for this exam since six o'clock this morning.
examQuestions.explanation: An activity that started in the past (*since six o'clock*) and continues up to now → **have been studying**.

examQuestions.text: There's so much traffic. By the time we get to the stadium, the match ___.
examQuestions.explanation: Completed before a future moment (*by the time we get there*) → **will have started**.

examQuestions.prompt: Complete with the correct form of the verb in brackets.
examQuestions.text: If you ___ (tell) me about the problem earlier, I could have helped you.
answers: had told
examQuestions.explanation: Third conditional if-clause → **had told** (+ *could have helped*).

examQuestions.prompt: Rewrite the situation as a conditional sentence.
examQuestions.sentence: I didn't bring my umbrella, so I'm wet now.
examQuestions.cue: Begin with: If I had brought ...
answers: If I had brought my umbrella, I wouldn't be wet now.
If I had brought my umbrella, I would not be wet now.
If I had brought my umbrella, I wouldn't be wet.
If I had brought my umbrella, I would not be wet.
examQuestions.explanation: Past condition (*had brought*) + present result (*now*) → mixed conditional: **I wouldn't be wet now**.
The shopping centre receives the action, and it is in progress → present continuous passive: **is being built**.

examQuestions.prompt: Which sentences describe a service that SOMEONE ELSE did for the subject? Select all that apply.
examQuestions.explanation: The causative **have/get + object + past participle** shows that someone else did the job.

examQuestions.text: The manager apologised ___ the mistake and promised ___ it again.

examQuestions.sentence: "I'll help you with the move," Pedro said to me.
answers: Pedro offered to help me with the move.
Pedro offered to help with the move.
examQuestions.explanation: **offer + to-infinitive**: *Pedro offered to help me with the move.*

examQuestions.context: The Grand Pelangi Hotel, ___ was built in 1920, has been beautifully restored.
examQuestions.explanation: A thing in a non-defining clause (between commas) → **which**. *That* is not allowed after a comma.

examQuestions.prompt: Put the words in the correct order.
examQuestions.explanation: Reduced passive relative clause: *The students **invited to the ceremony** were all from local schools.*

examQuestions.prompt: Complete using the words in brackets.
examQuestions.text: Lina isn't answering her phone. She ___ (might / leave) it at home.
answers: might have left

examQuestions.prompt: What does the phrase in bold mean?
examQuestions.context: After examining the car, the police have **ruled out** an accident.
options: They have decided that it was not an accident.
They have proved that it was an accident.
They are still investigating the accident.
examQuestions.explanation: **Rule out** = decide that something is not possible (mengesampingkan kemungkinan).

examQuestions.prompt: Complete the text with words from the bank.
examQuestions.text: ___ the heavy traffic, we arrived on time. We had left early ___ that we could find a parking space. ___, the meeting started late anyway!
answers: Despite
so
However
examQuestions.explanation: **Despite** + noun; **so that** + clause (purpose); **However,** links two sentences. *Although* would need a clause.

examQuestions.source: Saya menyesal tidak belajar bahasa Inggris lebih awal.
answers: I wish I had learned English earlier.
I wish I had learnt English earlier.
I wish I'd learned English earlier.
I wish I'd learnt English earlier.
I regret not learning English earlier.
I regret not having learned English earlier.
I regret not having learnt English earlier.
I regret that I didn't learn English earlier.
I wish I had started learning English earlier.
I wish I had studied English earlier.
I regret not studying English earlier.
If only I had learned English earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Director
dialogue.text: Have you made a decision about the new supplier?

options: Not yet. We need to take the delivery costs into account first.
Not yet. We need to take into the delivery costs account first.
Not yet. We need to make the delivery costs into account first.
Not yet. We need to do account of the delivery costs first.

examQuestions.prompt: Complete with ONE word: "In her new job, Sinta is responsible ___ training all new staff."
answers: for

placementQuestions.context: So you're still at the same company? How long ___ there?
placementQuestions.explanation: Duration up to now → present perfect continuous: **have you been working**.

placementQuestions.context: If I ___ about the train strike, I would have taken a taxi.
placementQuestions.explanation: Third conditional if-clause → past perfect: **had known**.

placementQuestions.prompt: Complete with the passive form of the verb in brackets.
placementQuestions.text: The bridge ___ (repair) at the moment, so the road is closed.
answers: is being repaired
placementQuestions.explanation: Action in progress + passive → **is being repaired**.

placementQuestions.text: The minister denied ___ the secret documents.

placementQuestions.context: Despite ___ very tired, she finished the marathon.
You ___ have told me you were moving house. I would have helped!
placementQuestions.explanation: Criticism of something that didn't happen → **should have told**.

placementQuestions.text: I'd rather you ___ my laptop without asking.
placementQuestions.explanation: **would rather + subject + past simple**: *I'd rather you didn't use...*

placementQuestions.prompt: What does the phrase in bold mean?
placementQuestions.context: After a difficult year, the company had to **cut costs**.
placementQuestions.explanation: **Cut costs** = reduce the amount of money spent.
*That* cannot be used in a non-defining relative clause; use **who** for people.

placementQuestions.context: It was ___ that we stayed at home all weekend.
placementQuestions.explanation: *Weather* is uncountable, so: **such + adjective + uncountable noun** → *such bad weather* (no *a*).
